messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh, an 18-year-old South Eastern Asian American man who worked as a photographer, came to treatment after months of feeling as though the war had never really ended. He had been deployed as a young combat photographer, carrying a camera and helmet through streets that could turn dangerous in seconds, and the memory that stayed with him most vividly was the day he filmed an ambush from behind a low wall while others ran for cover. He could still see the dust hanging in the air, hear the sharp crack of gunfire, and remember the moment a fellow soldier he had been standing near only minutes before was hit. What haunts Minh is not only what happened, but how real it remains to him: when he thinks back, the scene comes back with a force that feels more immediate than ordinary memory, as if it is happening again rather than being remembered.

After he returned home, Minh found himself thinking again and again that he should have protected the others and failed. He had been trained to observe and record, but in his mind that never excused what he felt he had not done. He came to believe that people cannot be trusted, because in combat the ground could look safe one moment and become lethal the next, and that he no longer belonged anywhere because neither civilian life nor the military felt fully like home anymore. Those beliefs settled quickly into the way he moved through daily life. At work, while photographing events and street scenes, he kept scanning crowds and doorways, certain that danger could appear without warning. Even in supposedly safe places, he could not relax. He sat with his shoulders tight, listening too hard for sudden noises, and ordinary sounds—a dropped metal case in the studio, a car backfiring outside, a phone banging against a table—could make him jump sharply before he could think. The more he saw the world as unsafe and people as unreliable, the more he stayed braced for attack.

That constant alertness pulled his memory along with it. When Minh was on edge, the war came back faster and more vividly, not as a distant recollection but as a full sensory return. A smell of hot pavement near a construction site, the pop of a balloon at a birthday shoot, or the sight of a narrow alley behind a venue could instantly bring back the battlefield without warning, and once that happened he would be flooded with the same rage he felt in combat. He would clench his jaw and replay the ambush in his mind, furious at the chaos, at the people who had been killed, and at himself for not being able to stop it. Those memories, in turn, made his beliefs harsher. The more real they felt, the more convinced he became that he truly had failed, that trust was dangerous, and that he was cut off from everyone around him. In that state he pushed himself into riskier behavior, taking chances he would never have taken before—driving too fast after a shoot, climbing unstable structures for a better angle, staying out alone too late—partly because he felt numb and partly because, in his own words, if danger was going to find him anyway, he might as well not be careful. 

Over the following months, Minh built his life around avoiding the moments that could set him off, but that strategy narrowed his world. He kept working as a photographer, yet he took jobs that felt less exposed and turned down assignments that involved crowds, loud events, or places with echoes and sudden movement. Even then, the effort to stay controlled only made him more tense; the more he watched for danger, the less able he was to settle, and the more often the memories broke through. He found himself isolated from friends, certain they would not understand what he had seen or why he still felt responsible. When he looked at himself, he saw not a young man home from service but someone who had no place and could not be trusted to keep others safe. After several especially bad weeks in which startle reactions, sleepless vigilance, and reckless choices began affecting his work and leaving him frightened of his own mind, Minh finally sought help because he was tired of feeling trapped between the certainty that he had failed and the fear that the war could return to him at any moment through the smallest sound or image. What he most hopes for now is relief from the vividness of those memories and the chance to believe, again, that he can belong somewhere without being on guard every second.
